Bowl-shaped conductive filler enabled low-modulus conductive ionic elastomer for conformal and efficient near-field electromagnetic shielding
abstract: Lightweight and conformable electromagnetic interference (EMI) shielding materials are highly desirable for wearable communication and embodied artificial intelligence. However, simultaneously achieving extremely high electrical conductivity and low modulus in conductive elastomers remains a significant challenge. Herein, a novel bowl-shaped silver-coated expanded polymer beads (Ag@EBs) incorporated polyvinyl alcohol/phytic acid (PVA/PhA) conductive ionic elastomer with silver/ion dual conductive network structure is fabricated for conformal and highly efficient near-field (NF) EMI shielding. The bowl-shaped Ag@EBs, featuring an open-ended architecture, enable dense in-plane stacking to form the primary conductive network and can readily deform with the soft PVA/PhA ionic elastomer matrix. Meanwhile, H⁺ ions released from the PhA moieties serve as a synergistic ionic conductive pathway, reducing the contact resistance between adjacent Ag@EBs and thereby stabilizing the conductive network. As a result, the prepared composite film exhibited a rather low modulus of only 299 kPa and an exceptional EMI shielding effectiveness (SE) of 92.6 dB at the thickness of only ~200 μm. Notably, the dual-conductive network also ensured the stable conductivity of the elastomer even under large deformation, with only a negligible decrease at a tensile strain of ~200%. Owing to its soft and robustly conductive characteristics, the film exhibits excellent conformability to complex surfaces and achieves a remarkable near-field EMI shielding effectiveness (NF-SE) of -53.28 dB, comparable to that of copper foil shields. Our work provides a new strategy for designing conformable EMI shielding materials which are highly promising for conferring reliable NF shielding to stretchable and wearable electronics

title: Physics-informed data-driven topology-supported precursor screening strategy for designing all-organic polyimide dielectrics with deep traps and wide-temperature-range
Explainable reinforcement learning designs a LRP1-targeted BBB-penetrating peptide with spatial selectivity for glioblastoma therapy
Integrating machine learning and CFD-derived hydrodynamics for predictive scale-up of combined cooling and antisolvent crystallization
abstract: Scale-up of crystallization processes remains a major challenge due to the complex interplay between operating conditions, hydrodynamics, and particle-level phenomena. This study presents an interpretable machine learning framework for predicting product particle size distributions (PSD) in a combined cooling and antisolvent crystallization process across laboratory and pilot scales. Partial least squares (PLS) regression models with bootstrapping-based uncertainty quantification were constructed using three categories of input variables: (i) operating conditions alone, (ii) operating conditions with empirical hydrodynamic descriptors, and (iii) operating conditions with both empirical and CFD-derived hydrodynamic descriptors. At small scales (400 mL, 500 mL, and 3 L), both (ii) and (iii) improved predictive accuracy relative to (i), with consistent performance across train–test splits. For extrapolation to mid-scale (5 L) and large-scale (100 L) crystallizers, only models including CFD-derived hydrodynamic features provided accurate predictions, demonstrating their critical role in scale-up. The variable importance scores of the PLS models revealed the key operational and hydrodynamic factors that influence PSD predictions across scales. The proposed framework offers a generalizable digital design tool aiding scale-up of crystallization processes, integrating mechanistic hydrodynamic insights with machine learning to enable predictive, data-efficient, and interpretable scale-up.

title: Electron beam and protease–induced modifications of ECM protein hydrogels: Collagen- and elastin-specific structural insights via fast green staining and fluorescence lifetime CLSM
abstract: Collagen–elastin hydrogels have gained increasing attention as versatile extracellular matrix-based biomaterials for tissue engineering, drug delivery, and regenerative medicine. Their tunable mechanical properties, inherent biocompatibility, and responsiveness to external cues make them ideal yet complex systems for biomedical applications. Recent studies have demonstrated that high-energy electron beam irradiation offers a reagent-free approach for crosslinking collagen-elastin hydrogels, enabling precise modulation of network density, mechanical behavior, and thermo-responsiveness under sterilizing conditions. To better understand and visualize the effects of electron beam treatment and enzymatic degradation on the microarchitecture of these hybrid materials we employed fluorescence lifetime-based confocal laser scanning microscopy combined with Fast Green staining. This technique enabled the simultaneous differentiation of collagen and elastin subnetworks at the fibrillar level and facilitated the investigation of the behavior of individual protein components during radiation-chemical processing, enzymatic degradation, and combinations thereof. Electron beam treated and untreated gels were exposed to selective enzymatic degradation using trypsin and elastase, providing insights into the proteolytic stability of the individual matrix components. Lifetime based imaging revealed significant differences in collagen and elastin susceptibility to enzymatic cleavage following electron beam treatment. To support the analysis, machine learning-based segmentation was applied, with a primary focus on voxel-wise classification using the 3D pixel classifier in AIVIA, allowing for a volumetric and spatially resolved characterization of the datasets. The findings highlight the potential of fluorescence lifetime-based confocal laser scanning microscopy and machine learning-based image analysis for characterization of extracellular matrix-mimetic biomaterials and their dynamic remodeling behavior, with implications for optimizing scaffold design in bioengineering applications.

title: Molecular engineering of CRISPR biosensors: From rational design to AI acceleration
Machine learning assisted identification of MOF-derived ZnO/In dual gas sensor activated by blue light at near room temperature
Interfacial polarity regulation enables robust self-healing conductive elastomers for wearable motion recognition
abstract: Flexible strain sensors must withstand repeated deformation while preserving mechanical integrity, autonomous repairability, and stable signal transduction. Conductive polymer composites, however, often suffer from filler aggregation and fragile conductive networks, making it difficult to reconcile strength, self-healing capability, and sensing reliability. Here, we report an interfacial polarity regulation strategy to construct a self-healing conductive elastomer composed of furan-functionalized carbon nanotubes and Diels–Alder-crosslinked epoxidized natural rubber (ECNT). Molecular simulations, together with spectroscopic and morphological analyses, reveal that the furan-regulated interface generates localized polar domains and accessible interaction sites, thereby promoting nanotube dispersion and interfacial coupling within the elastomer matrix. The optimized ECNT-2 composite achieves a tensile strength of 7.74 MPa, an elongation at break of 467%, and a self-healing efficiency above 90% after thermal treatment. Enabled by dynamic conductive-network reconstruction and reversible covalent crosslinking, the elastomer sensor delivers a gauge factor of 3.76, response/recovery times below 180/140 ms, and stable piezoresistive signals under cyclic deformation. It reliably monitors large joint motions and subtle physiological activities, including finger bending, elbow flexion, coughing, and smiling. Coupled with a one-dimensional convolutional neural network, the sensor achieves window-level validation accuracies of 100% for representative motions and 98.7% for finger gestures, supporting robotic-hand teleoperation. This work links molecular-level polarity engineering with intelligent wearable sensing, offering a rational route to robust self-healing conductive elastomers for adaptive human-machine interfaces.

title: The cathode–electrolyte interphase meets artificial intelligence: From formation and evolution mechanisms to data-driven interphase design
Machine learning strategies integrating knowledge transfer and a cascaded framework: Guiding the discovery of NIR-II organic cocrystals
abstract: Organic cocrystals represent a highly promising class of photothermal materials operating in the near-infrared second (NIR-II) window. However, efficient identification and rational design remain challenging due to the vast chemical space and the complex, nontrivial relationships between molecular structures and functional properties. In this work, we develop a cascaded dual-task (C2T) machine learning (ML) framework that effectively links cocrystal-formability recognition (M1) with NIR-II absorption identification (M2) through feature knowledge transfer. We constructed the first hierarchical organic cocrystal database, comprising 2,648 cocrystal samples and 128 NIR-II cocrystals. By integrating RDKit and PaDEL descriptors to generate dual-representation molecular features, a dual-task prediction model is established. Under small-sample conditions, both M1 and M2 achieve high predictive accuracies (>92%) and demonstrate strong generalization capabilities. Guided by the model, we discover and experimentally validate the DPQ cocrystals, which exhibits intense NIR-II absorption (up to 1200 nm) and efficient photothermal behavior (~120℃@1024 nm). Moreover, multiscale theoretical calculations combined with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based model interpretability elucidate the structure-property relationships from molecular architecture to macroscopic performance. This work demonstrates the potential of ML for precise cocrystal design and efficient performance identification under small-sample conditions, paving the way for ML-accelerated development of functional molecular materials.

title: Vacancy–metal–site coupling in defective MgO-supported single-atom catalysts for CO2-to-CO reduction: DFT screening assisted by multimodal transfer learning
Redox-active coordination catalysts for selective thermochemical valorization of biowaste: Mechanistic insights and structure-performance relationships
abstract: The growing demand for renewable energy has intensified global efforts to transform biowastes into value-added fuels and chemicals rather than viewing them as disposal challenges. Derived mainly from lignocellulosic and other organic residues, these wastes are rich in carbon and reactive functional groups, making them promising feedstocks for thermochemical conversion via pyrolysis, gasification, and hydrothermal liquefaction. Yet, their compositional complexity, high oxygen content, and inorganic impurities remain major barriers to efficient transformation and catalyst durability. This review offers an integrated perspective on recent advances in the catalytic valorization of biowaste, with a particular emphasis on how coordination chemistry principles can enhance reaction selectivity and energy efficiency. Redox-active metal complexes, zeolites, and metal-organic frameworks are highlighted for their ability to mediate controlled bond activation and electron transfer during reforming and aromatization processes. By linking feedstock chemistry, pretreatment strategies, and catalytic mechanisms, this work establishes structure-activity-selectivity relationships that underpin syngas and aromatic production. Finally, emerging concepts such as AI-guided catalyst design, integration with circular bioeconomy frameworks, and dual-function redox systems, are discussed as promising pathways toward scalable, low-carbon, and sustainable energy technologies.

title: Machine learning-guided design of glycosaminoglycans composite fiber scaffolds for neuro-osteogenic regeneration
abstract: Repairing large bone defects caused by trauma or disease poses a significant clinical challenge. Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), major components of organic matrix, play a crucial role in osteogenesis. Here, we report a machine learning (ML)-guided strategy for enhancing the design of osteogenic multicomponent GAGs. First, we constructed a dataset of 169/173 data for cell differentiation and viability of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs) cultured on different GAGs formulations to build an optimal formulation screening model through random forest (RF) and XGBoost (XGB) algorithms. We efficiently screened 59 good GAGs from 10,000 formulations generated in the whole space that own maximized cell differentiation and viability through the model. Based on cell mineralization activity, secondary screening identified 3 optimal formulations (GAG3–5). Based on these formulations, optimal formulation GAGs adsorbed into magnesium doped amino modified mesoporous bioactive glass (MBG) as the core, nerve growth factor (NGF) adsorbed into silk fibroin (SF) as the shell to form a composite fiber MBG/GAG@SF/NGF scaffold through coaxial electrospinning. Interestingly, we observed that MBG/GAG3,5@SF/NGF scaffolds promoted the osteogenesis process by activating the Bone morphogenetic protein 2 (Bmp2)/Smad and p-Erk1/2 signaling pathways in vitro . Furthermore, we found that MBG/GAG3,5@SF/NGF scaffolds enhanced the neurogenesis process in vitro . Intriguingly, we also observed that MBG/GAG5@SF/NGF scaffold effectively guided functional bone regeneration accompanied with enhanced neurogenesis and angiogenesis in mouse cranial defect model in vivo . This study not only provides an efficient MBG/GAG5@SF/NGF composite fiber multifunctional scaffold for bone defect repair but also establishes a scalable paradigm for ML-guided screening of bioactive formulations.

title: AI-accelerated hybrid reactive-nonreactive molecular dynamics simulation for polymer cross-linking
abstract: Molecular dynamics simulation based on reactive forcefield enables atomic-scale investigation of polymer cross-linking processes but is limited by high computational cost. In polymer cross-linking simulations, a large fraction of simulation time is spent in chemically inactive stages, during which the continuous use of a reactive forcefield is inefficient. In this work, an artificial intelligence-accelerated hybrid reactive-nonreactive molecular dynamics framework is developed, which adaptively switches between reactive and non-reactive forcefields to improve computational efficiency while maintaining chemical accuracy. A machine learning model is trained on reactive molecular dynamics trajectories to predict continuous reaction probability using physically interpretable structural, chemical, and energetic descriptors extracted from simulation outputs. This probabilistic criterion enables reliable identification of low-reactivity states and stable forcefield switching without manually defined heuristic rules. The proposed approach is applied to the cross-linking process of epoxy as a representative example. Compared with full reactive forcefield simulations, the hybrid approach achieves up to 80% reduction in computational cost. Structural and mechanical properties of the cross-linked epoxy network obtained from the hybrid simulations show excellent agreement with full reactive forcefield results and experimental reference data. This work provides a framework that accelerates polymer cross-linking simulations while preserving key reaction chemistry, network evolution, and final material properties. Using epoxy-amine cross-linking as a representative case, the study establishes a proof-of-concept strategy for coupling chemically faithful reactive sampling with efficient nonreactive relaxation. The framework may be extended to other reaction-relaxation systems after system-specific descriptor construction, threshold calibration, and independent validation.

title: AI-assisted molecular and materials discovery in chemistry and chemical engineering: A methodological and bibliometric review
Physics-informed neural network reconstructions of free surfaces and flow fields from sparse data in turbulent regimes, with applications in stirred tanks
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are a promising meshless framework for fluid dynamics, capable of solving both forward and inverse problems, and incorporating observational data into the model. However, their application to coupled multiphase turbulent flows remains limited, particularly in industrial inverse problems, where measurements may be sparse, expensive, and are often devoid of turbulence values. In this work, we develop a PINN framework for reconstructing the free surface, along with the velocity and pressure fields from sparse data, and test it on a mixing tank. Models are trained on limited velocity and pressure data from a time-averaged, axisymmetric CFD reference simulation. The data are free of direct measurements from the free surface or turbulence terms. Models are evaluated across varying impeller speeds and fluid viscosities. Both laminar and turbulent models are tested, including with eddy viscosity closures and anisotropic stresses. A Spalart–Allmaras turbulence closure is used, while including anisotropic stresses can improve the pressure and free surface predictions. From as few as 25 measurement locations, models are able to reconstruct, with low error, the velocity and pressure fields, and the final model achieves average free-surface errors below 1 mm in all tested operating conditions relative to a CFD reference. Additionally, models can accurately detect features such as additional vortices, jet splitting and impingement regions.

title: Physics-informed LSTM for lignocellulosic pyrolysis kinetics at elevated heating rates: Integrating Arrhenius constraints with data-driven modeling
AI-assisted design of metal-organic frameworks for hydrogen storage: From databases to generative models
abstract: Nowadays, the development of a sustainable hydrogen economy and the widespread deployment of high-capacity hydrogen storage for hydrogen vehicles and energy systems are of great importance. Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), with their diverse structures, have emerged as the most promising materials for next-generation gas storage due to their high surface area, tunable pore size, and diversity of chemical bonds. However, the fabrication of MOF materials through manual experimental screening is very time-consuming and costly. Recently, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) algorithms, combined with quantum databases, advanced modeling, and screening strategies for discovering MOF structures, have revolutionized materials science. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in AI-assisted discovery of novel MOF materials specifically for hydrogen storage applications. We present MOF databases, modeling strategies based on material structure descriptors and materials discovery, large language model (LLM) algorithms for automated data mining, and ML-assisted force fields (FFs) at the atomic level for hydrogen storage. Furthermore, we discuss key challenges such as data quality, model transferability, and discrepancies between simulations and experiments. Finally, this review paper outlines future prospects for this rapidly evolving interdisciplinary field, with an emphasis on advancing MOF materials discovery through accurate AI models.

title: Artificial intelligence-driven glycosaminoglycan-mimetic polymer design for cartilage regeneration
Deciphering the water-thermal stability trade-offs via interpretable machine learning for reliable design of dual-stable MOFs
Ultrasound-enhanced goethite coprecipitation for synergistic enrichment of Ga, Ge and In: A combined molecular dynamics, artificial neural network and EXAFS study
Unveiling the atomic scale synthesis dynamics of lithium thiophosphate electrolytes via machine learning interatomic potentials
NanoChef: AI framework for simultaneous optimization of synthesis sequences and reaction conditions at autonomous laboratories
abstract: We present NanoChef , a deep learning-based framework for the simultaneous optimization of synthesis sequences and reaction conditions in autonomous laboratories. Unlike traditional AI models focused solely on continuous variables, NanoChef incorporates positional encoding and MatBERT embedding to represent reagent sequences as vectorized inputs, enabling joint modeling of sequential and continuous variables in nanoparticle (NP) synthesis. In virtual experiments, NanoChef consistently searched for the best-identified optimum across synthesis-order-sensitive landscapes in under 40 cycles. Despite the complexity of 17.5 billion candidate recipes driven by 24 possible sequences in a four-reagent system, this framework achieved an optimal recipe for Ag NP synthesis, characterized by a λ max of 513 nm and a 36% reduction in full width at half maximum within fewer than 350 experiments. This search efficiency was underscored by the reductant-last strategy, which consistently yielded optimal results across all permutations of two- to four-reagent systems. Additionally, NanoChef newly discovered an oxidant–last strategy that produces monodisperse NPs on average. By optimizing both continuous volume and the order of reagent addition, the framework redefines synthesis order as a tunable design variable and demonstrates how AI can accelerate autonomous chemistry while handling high-dimensional combinatorial challenges that exceed the capabilities of fixed-order methods.

title: Role of artificial intelligence and machine learning techniques in pyrolytic liquefaction of biomass and waste polymers: From mechanistic insights to process automation
Towards generalizable wet foamability predictions: A dimensional analysis approach incorporating dynamic surface tension and symbolic regression
abstract: This study presents a groundbreaking chemical engineering approach to modeling wet foam formation through mechanical mixing and gas-sparging processes. Situated at the intersection of physico-chemistry, dimensional analysis, chemical engineering, and predictive modeling, this work utilizes an extensive experimental dataset covering a broad spectrum of operating conditions.For each foaming process examined, a single dimensionless correlation – capable of accurately predicting foam heights – is derived, irrespective of surfactant type, provided that dynamic surface tension is explicitly accounted for. The findings emphasize the pivotal role of surfactant dynamics in macroscopic foaming behavior, demonstrating that the time-dependent evolution of surface tension must be incorporated into foaming process models. This study serves as a compelling example of how chemical engineering principles can bridge molecular-scale mechanisms (e.g., surfactant migration at bubble interfaces) with macroscopic physical variables (e.g., foam height) observed at the process scale.Beyond its immediate relevance to the foaming community, this work highlights the feasibility of integrating non-constant properties into dimensional analysis frameworks – a practice rarely applied in the chemical engineering field – while adhering to rigorous similarity theory principles. Most importantly, the study underscores a broader message for chemical engineers: modern semi-empirical correlations can achieve unprecedented robustness by synergistically combining dimensional analysis (retaining physical interpretability and scalability, unlike purely data-driven approaches) with AI-driven techniques.

title: Machine learning-integrated wearable sensors for intelligent disease diagnosis and personalized healthcare
From molecular discovery to system management: A mini-review on machine learning driving full-cycle optimization of aqueous flow batteries
From molecular generation to process-relevant performance: AI-driven identification of novel working fluids
abstract: The search for working fluids that balance thermodynamic performance, safety, and environmental sustainability remains a pressing challenge for refrigeration and heat pump technologies. Here, we present a hybrid computational workflow combining deep generative learning with classical thermodynamic modelling to identify novel working fluid candidates. Using a graph-based diffusion model, we generate and screen molecules against a quantitative physicochemical profile derived from known working fluids. We characterise five selected candidates in depth through molecular dynamics simulations, the polar soft-SAFT equation of state, COSMO-RS calculations, and two neural network predictors for flammability and GWP. We find that the predicted thermophysical and transport properties of the candidates fall within the range of established hydrofluorocarbons. Benchmarking against R-245fa and R-134a identifies a new compound (3,3,3-trifluoro-2-methylpropene) as the most promising candidate for high-temperature heat pump applications, and confirms another (1,1,1,2,2-pentafluoropropane) as a viable refrigerant for vapour compression cycles. Our work establishes a scalable framework for the rational, data-driven discovery of next-generation working fluids.

title: Combining physics-informed machine learning and heterogeneous transfer learning for hydrodenitrogenation of co-processed feedstocks
abstract: Accurately predicting the nitrogen content of co-processed petroleum feedstocks after hydrotreatment is a common challenge in refining, exacerbated by the limited experimental data available for each new feedstock. Transfer learning addresses this scarcity by leveraging knowledge from a related, data-rich source. For the source, the hydrodenitrogenation (HDN) of fossil vacuum gas oil, a rich dataset and an accurate prior ordinary differential equation (ODE) are available; for the target, the HDN of co-processed vacuum gas oil and tire-pyrolysis oil, the ODE structure is unknown and an additional descriptor (the tire fraction) is present, making the problem heterogeneous. To recover this unknown ODE, we propose HTL-HyODE, a heterogeneous transfer learning hybrid ODE in which small neural networks encode its unknown components while the rest is kept explicit and transferred from the source. For comparison, we also develop physics-informed variants (HTL-PINNs) of data-driven heterogeneous transfer networks. On simulated data, HTL-HyODE reduces the test mean absolute error (MAE) by up to 52% relative to a no-transfer hybrid baseline at a training size of n t = 25 when the networks are correctly placed. On experimental data, the benefit with respect to the no-transfer hybrid baseline depends on the target size and on the retained structure: at n t = 15 the best-matched structure reduces the MAE by about 50%–57%, whereas at n t = 50 the data-driven and physics-informed networks overtake it, DHTLFT-PINNs reaching the lowest error. Embedding the kinetic structure explicitly is thus most effective when it is reliable and data are scarce, while network-based transfer becomes preferable as data accumulate; the learned hybrid components remain physically consistent in both regimes.

title: Engineering precision antimicrobials: AI-driven design of self-assembling non-natural peptide nanostructures
Fast parameter identification for elementary-step surface mechanisms using kinetically parameterized neural networks
abstract: Microkinetic models provide physically grounded descriptions of catalytic systems. However, quantitative prediction of catalyst performance requires refinement of elementary-step parameters against reactor-level measurement data. This calibration is computationally demanding because it involves repeated reactor simulations with computationally expensive microkinetic models. Surrogates that approximate the kinetic model reduce evaluation cost, but are currently tied to fixed kinetic parameters and therefore cannot be used for mechanism calibration. To address this limitation, we introduce kinetically parameterized Global Reaction Neural Network (pGRNN) surrogates that map both operating conditions and elementary-step kinetic parameters of a detailed microkinetic mechanism to species source terms. By embedding stoichiometry, thermodynamic consistency, and elementary-step structure, the surrogate replaces expensive kinetics evaluations while retaining a mechanism-consistent representation. Using the preferential CO oxidation on platinum, we show that the pGRNN predicts source terms across a broad range of operating conditions and kinetic parameters with a relative error of 1.2%. Reactor model evaluation is accelerated by a factor of 3100. The pGRNN is used in place of the kinetic model during mechanism calibration, reducing calibration time by factors of approximately 2400 for a synthetic single light-off curve and a synthetic multi-experiment campaign. Finally, we demonstrate the workflow by efficiently calibrating the mechanism against measured reactor-performance data from two experimental setups. A differentiable implementation of kinetic and reactor model further enables efficient gradient-based calibration. The proposed workflow provides an accelerated route for adapting detailed microkinetic models to catalyst-specific performance data.
